title: The Last Signal
notes: v5 expansion: added DP-level sub-locations for every location the script visits with camera presence, added missing props the script gives narrative weight to, and added two new top-level locations (Betty Klenck home, National Archives) that v4 omitted entirely. All v4 entries preserved unchanged.

assets.name: Amelia_Earhart_1937
assets.notes: Age 39. World circumnavigation attempt. Pilot of the Lockheed Electra NR16020. Her voice is heard at S-five signal strength — maximum — in the Itasca radio log. She is transmitting but cannot hear the Itasca. Last known transmission at 0843 on July 2, 1937.

assets.name: Frederick_Noonan_1937
assets.physique: American man, mid-40s, lean build, clean-shaven with a broad jaw, steady unhurried hands trained by decades of precision instrument work, sharp navigational eyes that assess distance habitually, the composed bearing of a man who has spent his career finding small islands in large oceans
assets.attire: Aviation working clothes for a long Pacific crossing — cotton shirt, lightweight trousers, leather belt, practical lace-up shoes; possibly a light jacket for altitude cold
assets.notes: The most experienced Pacific aerial navigator alive in 1937. Charted the Pan American transpacific Clipper routes. Sat behind the bulkhead for the entire 20-hour Lae-to-Howland flight. Communicated with Earhart by handwritten note through the partition gap. Married Mary Beatrice Martinelli on March 27, 1937 — two months before the flight. His final calculation: sun line 157/337 degrees. Never appears in the radio transmissions; his voice is not in the Itasca log. He is in the numbers.

assets.name: Leo_Bellarts_1937
assets.physique: American man, mid-20s, lean and alert with the keyed-up posture of a man who has been wearing headphones for eight hours straight, dark circles under watchful eyes, the economical movement of someone who has worked ships long enough to navigate tight spaces without thinking about it
assets.attire: United States Coast Guard enlisted working uniform — dark wool dress uniform or working khakis appropriate to 1937 shipboard duty, rank insignia of Radioman First Class
assets.notes: Chief radioman aboard the USCGC Itasca. On watch July 2, 1937. Logged Earhart's transmissions. Ran from the radio room to the bridge when the S-five signal arrived. Kept the original radio log for decades — not because required to, but because he understood what it contained. Donated it to the National Archives as the Leo G. Bellarts Papers, 1937-1971. Believed until death that Earhart was peacefully on the bottom of the sea, no farther than 100 miles from Howland.

assets.name: Thomas_OHare_1937
assets.physique: American man, early 20s, the slightly raw unfinished quality of a young enlisted man not yet fully settled into his body, alert dark eyes behind a face trained to reveal nothing while the mind behind it races, the unconscious posture of someone who has been listening hard for hours
assets.attire: United States Coast Guard enlisted working uniform — khakis or dark wool appropriate to 1937 shipboard duty, rank insignia of Radioman Third Class
assets.notes: Radioman Third Class on the Itasca's secondary receiver. Asked the question no official record answered: 'Why couldn't she hear me on three one oh five?' Monitored the frequency off-shift on personal equipment for two days after the disappearance. Filed a report on a possible voice transmission at 0300 on July 4. The duty officer logged it as atmospheric skip. O'Hare's diary, July 4: 'It was not skip. I have been listening to skip for four years. Skip does not say words.'

assets.name: Gerald_Gallagher_1940
assets.physique: Irish man, 26-27 years old, lean build appropriate to a colonial posting in a tropical climate, an administrative bearing that reads as younger than his authority — the earnest precision of a man who does his job thoroughly because he believes it matters, not because he is watched
assets.attire: British colonial administrative dress — lightweight cotton trousers and shirt appropriate to tropical Pacific posting, leather belt and shoes, possibly a light canvas jacket
assets.notes: British colonial administrator assigned to Nikumaroro (Gardner Island) to oversee Gilbertese resettlement scheme. Found partial human remains on the southeastern shore in September 1940, with a woman's shoe, a man's shoe, a sextant box, and a Benedictine bottle. His official report named Earhart explicitly. Died on the island in September 1941, age 29, of illness. His personal letter to his sister describes numbers scratched into a tree trunk — 157 and 337 — which he copied without knowing what a sun line was.

assets.name: DW_Hoodless_1940
assets.physique: British colonial physician, mid-40s, professional bearing with the careful neutral expression of a medical examiner, methodical precise hands, the slight formality of a man operating within an institutional system that prizes accurate record-keeping above all else
assets.attire: Colonial British professional dress — light linen suit or cotton trousers with a collared shirt, appropriate to Fiji's tropical climate
assets.notes: Physician in Fiji who examined the skeletal remains sent from Nikumaroro. His conclusion: stocky, middle-aged male. Not Earhart. The bones were subsequently lost. His written measurements — bone lengths, widths, ratios — survived and became the only physical evidence the case retains. Two 21st-century forensic analyses of his numbers reached opposite conclusions.

assets.name: Richard_Jantz_2018
assets.physique: American man, late 70s, the lean slightly stooped build of a senior academic, wire-rimmed reading glasses, the unhurried deliberate movement of someone whose professional authority is earned and does not need to be announced
assets.attire: Academic casual dress — khaki trousers, collared shirt, perhaps a blazer
assets.notes: Forensic anthropologist at the University of Tennessee. Applied the FORDISC method to Hoodless's 1940 bone measurements in 2018. Conclusion: the measurements were more consistent with a woman of Earhart's proportions than 99% of individuals in the reference sample. Not a match — a probability. His analysis and the 2015 Cross/Wright analysis point in opposite directions from the same set of numbers. The bones are gone. There is no third measurement possible.

assets.name: Betty_Klenck_1937
assets.physique: American girl, 15 years old, the alert curiosity of a teenager who spends time with a shortwave radio — a focused practical expression when listening, a hand moving steadily across notebook paper
assets.attire: 1930s American casual dress for a teenager at home — cotton dress or blouse and skirt, appropriate to Florida summer
assets.notes: Fifteen-year-old in Saint Petersburg, Florida. Was listening to her family's shortwave radio on 3105 kHz in the days after the disappearance. Heard a woman's voice and wrote what she believed she heard in a notebook. The notebook was not publicized for decades. Now held by a research organization investigating the disappearance. The content includes details she would have had no knowledge of in 1937 that researchers note are consistent with the known circumstances of the flight.

assets.name: NRL_Researcher_1953
assets.physique: American man, late 30s to early 40s, the indoor academic pallor of a government research scientist, methodical careful hands trained by precision instrument work, wire-rimmed glasses, the particular slightly distracted expression of someone whose professional attention is always partly on a problem
assets.attire: 1950s American professional dress — dark trousers, white shirt with tie, possibly a lab or office coat
assets.notes: Unnamed radio propagation researcher at the Naval Research Laboratory in Washington. Was working on a retrospective analysis of high-frequency radio propagation anomalies in the Pacific theater during WWII. His appendix analyzed the Earhart case as a documented asymmetric propagation event. Finding: atmospheric conditions on July 2-5, 1937 were normal. The asymmetry was not atmospheric in origin. His marginal note in pencil: 'Then what was it?' The study was never published. The appendix was excluded from partial declassification.

assets.name: USCGC_Itasca_1937
assets.physique: A United States Coast Guard Cutter — a 250-foot steam-powered ocean-going vessel, steel hull painted grey-white with Coast Guard markings, single stack amidships emitting a column of black-grey smoke used as a visual marker. The ship is anchored off the western shore of Howland Island in the central Pacific. Low Pacific swells. Morning cumulus. The smoke column bending southeast in the wind.
assets.notes: Assigned to serve as radio communications ship and visual landmark for Earhart's arrival at Howland Island. Operating on 3105 kHz. Radiomen Bellarts and O'Hare both on duty. The ship transmitted at full power; the aircraft heard it only intermittently. The ship heard the aircraft at maximum signal strength but the sky above Howland Island remained empty.

children.name: Itasca_Radio_Room_1937
children.physique: A sealed compartment below the bridge level. Heated by the equipment itself — warm, close air smelling of electronics, brass fittings, and the accumulated exhalations of men awake for hours. A receiver desk with Bakelite headphones on a hook. A log sheet on the desk surface, slightly damp from Pacific humidity. A pencil resting beside it. The marks in the log slightly softer than dry paper — more decisive. Dial set to 3105 kHz. The needle of the signal strength meter visible. Brass hardware, painted steel walls, a single overhead lamp.
children.notes: Where Bellarts was sitting when the S-five signal arrived at 0742. He stood up, took the headphones off in one motion, and ran.

children.name: Itasca_Bridge_1937
children.physique: The open bridge of a Coast Guard cutter. Steel deck underfoot, the ring of hard soles on painted metal. The Pacific directly present — salt air, heat, thin chemical smell of stack smoke bending in the wind. The smoke column visible from here, rising and bending southeast. Howland Island visible to the east as a low profile barely distinguishable from the sea surface. Morning cumulus clouds, scattered, with open sky between them. The horizon in every direction: water.
children.notes: Where Bellarts ran after hearing the S-five transmission. He looked at the sky. The sky was empty. He will carry this moment for the rest of his life.

children.name: Itasca_Secondary_Receiver_Station_1937
children.physique: A secondary listening post aboard the Itasca — a companion station to the main radio room, positioned for redundant monitoring. A secondary receiver set, slightly older than the main desk equipment, with a second set of Bakelite headphones hanging from a metal hook. A blank report form on the desk surface, the kind used for operational monitoring logs. The dial set to 3105 kHz. The station has the quality of a space where a younger man works — less settled, more alert, a seabag visible in the corner. The hum of the ship's engine present through the steel deck.
children.notes: Where O'Hare was working during the watch on July 2, 1937. He was monitoring the secondary receiver. His question — 'Why couldn't she hear me on three one oh five?' — was asked here or in the debrief that followed. After his watch ended, he returned here with personal equipment and monitored off-shift for two days.

children.name: Itasca_Companionway_1937
children.physique: The narrow steep interior staircase of a Coast Guard cutter connecting the radio room level to the bridge level. Steel treads, painted grey, a single pipe rail on one side. The angle of the stairs close to 45 degrees — a ship's stair, not a building stair. The light at the top coming through the bridge hatchway. The sound of boots on steel, ascending fast.
children.notes: The path Bellarts ran when the S-five signal arrived. The script describes the sound specifically: 'the ring of boot soles on the companionway of a Coast Guard cutter — not the dull thud of a wooden deck, not the soft absorption of carpet, but the ring of hard soles on painted steel.' A transitional space that carries the weight of the decision to run.

assets.name: Lockheed_Electra_Cockpit_1937
assets.physique: The forward compartment of a Lockheed Model 10-E Electra, registration NR16020. Twin-engine aluminum aircraft, cockpit built for a single pilot. The instrument panel glowing in darkness: altimeter reading 1000 feet, airspeed indicator at approximately 145 mph, fuel gauges with needles drifted far left after 17 hours of flight. An artificial horizon gyroscope — the substitute for the absent real horizon below. The control column under the hands. The rudder pedals. Every surface vibrating with the chord of two Pratt and Whitney Wasp radials at cruise power. A wooden partition directly behind the pilot's seat with a narrow gap at the bottom — the gap through which handwritten notes are passed forward from the navigation space aft. The air smells of avgas, hydraulic fluid, and altitude cold.
assets.notes: Earhart's position for 20 hours. The fuel gauges are the clocks in this aircraft — measuring time in the irreversible mathematics of how long two engines can run on what remains. The window shows darkness and ocean, horizon indistinguishable from sky.

children.name: Electra_Instrument_Panel_Close_1937
children.physique: An extreme close study of the Lockheed Electra's instrument panel — the cluster of round dials set into dark-painted metal, each dial a world of its own. The altimeter: a white face with a sweep hand reading 1000 feet, the numbers around the dial in increments of 100. The airspeed indicator: 145 mph, the needle slightly below cruise, the aircraft running lean. The artificial horizon gyroscope: the horizon line level but the representation is a horizon that does not exist outside the aircraft. The fuel gauges — two of them, one per engine — their needles drifted far toward the left peg, toward empty. A clock. The instruments glow with the particular amber-grey of 1930s aircraft instrument lighting. Every surface around the instruments vibrates.
children.notes: The fuel gauges are the emotional center of this instrument panel. The script returns to them repeatedly: 'The fuel gauges are the clocks in this aircraft.' A DP shot of the panel with the fuel gauge needles left of center communicates the irreversibility of the situation without a word.

children.name: Electra_Partition_Gap_1937
children.physique: The wooden bulkhead that divides the Lockheed Electra's fuselage — viewed from the pilot's position looking aft, or from the navigation space looking forward. Raw painted wood, the surface vibrating with the engine chord. At the base of the partition: a narrow gap, perhaps 4-6 inches in height, running the width of the bulkhead. A folded slip of paper resting at the gap's edge, or being passed through. The note in Noonan's steady handwriting: two numbers. The gap is the only communication channel between pilot and navigator except shouting over two radial engines.
children.notes: The script makes this gap a significant object: 'Communication happens by note, passed forward through the gap.' The handwritten note with 157 and 337 was passed through this gap. Visually: a close shot of a hand passing a small folded paper through a gap in painted wood, while the wood vibrates.

children.name: Electra_Window_Over_Pacific_Night_1937
children.physique: The pilot's side window of the Lockheed Electra, viewed from inside the cockpit. The plexiglass or safety glass of a 1930s aircraft window, slightly curved, its surface carrying the vibration of the airframe. Beyond the glass: absolute darkness. Not the darkness of a room without lights — the darkness of the open Pacific at night from 1000 feet, where the water and the sky share the same color because there are no stars visible through the overcast and there is no moon and there is no land anywhere. The horizon does not exist. The window shows: nothing. The reflection in the glass: the faint glow of the instrument panel behind the pilot.
children.notes: The script is specific: 'nothing in the way that the Pacific announces itself: darkness absolute, and darkness, and the particular absence of any feature that would tell a human eye where the water ends and the sky begins.' The window is where Earhart is looking for Howland Island. The window shows nothing.

assets.name: Lockheed_Electra_Navigation_Space_1937
assets.physique: The aft fuselage compartment of the Lockheed Electra, separated from the cockpit by a wooden bulkhead. A small navigation table with charts spread and weighted against vibration. A bubble sextant — a precision instrument for taking star and sun shots when no true horizon exists. A chronometer for precise time measurement. A drift meter. Charts of the central Pacific. Noonan's handwriting on the charts: celestial calculation lines, position estimates, the sun line marked as two numbers — 157 and 337 degrees. The space is cold at altitude, vibrating continuously, close quarters. Communication with the pilot forward happens only by note through the gap in the partition.
assets.notes: Noonan's workspace for 20 hours. His steady hand — trained because unsteady hands produce numbers that end flights — produced the sun line that became the last coordinates Earhart reported on the radio.

children.name: Electra_Navigation_Table_1937
children.physique: The navigation table in the aft compartment of the Lockheed Electra — a small fold-down or fixed surface, sized for chart work in confined quarters. The surface covered by the central Pacific chart, its edges weighted with small objects to resist the vibration and turbulence. On the chart: pencil lines of celestial working — position lines, dead reckoning tracks, the sun line drawn as a straight line through the area near Howland Island at two bearings, labeled in a steady hand: 157. 337. A parallel ruler. Dividers. A pencil worn to half-length. The chronometer in its box, lid open, face visible. Every surface vibrates continuously. The cold of altitude present in the quality of the light and the stiffness of the chart paper.
children.notes: Where Noonan produced the sun line. The script emphasizes the steadiness of his handwriting — 'trained to remain steady because unsteady hands produce numbers that end flights.' The table is where the last navigational certainty in the flight was produced.

children.name: Electra_Navigation_Space_Looking_Forward_1937
children.physique: The view forward from the navigation space toward the wooden partition — a cramped close space with the bulkhead filling the forward view, the gap at its base the only visual connection to the cockpit beyond. The instruments of navigation arranged on the table to one side. The aft window of the aircraft showing darkness. The sounds: two Pratt and Whitney radials at cruise power, entering through every surface. The close air of a sealed space at altitude — cold, smelling of avgas, hydraulic fluid, the particular quality of metal and rubber and the exhalations of a man who has been working for twenty hours.
children.notes: The isolation of Noonan's position. He cannot see Earhart. He cannot speak to her except by shouting over engines. He passes his work through a gap and waits. The view from this position is: a wooden wall, a narrow opening, and the sound of engines.

assets.name: Howland_Island_1937
assets.physique: A Pacific coral island less than a mile and a half long, half a mile wide, at its highest point ten feet above sea level. The terrain is flat, low — barely distinguishable from the ocean surface from altitude. Sparse vegetation of low coastal scrub, the color of bleached coral and salt-weathered green. A sandy beach along portions of the shoreline. The island sits at the equator, the morning light coming in at an angle that throws the flat terrain into shadow, making the coral hard to distinguish against the surface of the Pacific.
assets.notes: The target for the most difficult navigation shot in aviation history — finding a 1.5-mile strip of land at sea level in the central Pacific after a 2,243-nautical-mile overwater crossing. The USCGC Itasca is anchored off the western shore. The Electra never found it.

children.name: Howland_Island_Aerial_View_1937
children.physique: Howland Island from approximately 1000 feet altitude — the view Earhart would have had if she had found it. The island as it appears from low altitude in the central Pacific: a low pale strip against dark ocean, barely distinguishable from the sea surface at morning light, the equatorial sun angle throwing the flat coral terrain into shadow that makes the island merge with its own reflection. The Itasca visible off the western shore as a grey hull with a smoke column bending southeast — the smoke the only vertical element in an otherwise flat seascape. The reef line of the island's perimeter the brightest feature — white water against dark ocean. From above: very small. From 1000 feet at 145 mph: appearing only seconds before it would need to be under you to land.
children.notes: The view Earhart was trying to find. The script is precise about the difficulty: 'two miles of island, ten feet high, against the surface of a sea that has been colored by overcast to a shade not meaningfully different from coral at distance.' This shot establishes why she couldn't find it — not as commentary, but as direct visual evidence.

children.name: Howland_Island_Surface_1937
children.physique: The surface of Howland Island at sea level — the coral flat of the island's interior, pale bleached coral and sparse scrub vegetation, the surface rough and dry under equatorial sun. The horizon from the island's surface: ocean in every direction. The Itasca smoke column rising from the western side. The sky: morning cumulus clouds, scattered, with open sky between them. No aircraft visible. The smoke column rising and bending, signaling to a sky that contains nothing.
children.notes: The island's perspective on the search — the place the aircraft was trying to reach, described from the ground. The smoke column is doing everything it was placed there to do. The sky above it is empty.

assets.name: Nikumaroro_Island_1937
assets.physique: A coral atoll in the southern Phoenix Islands group, approximately 4.5 degrees south latitude, 174 degrees west longitude. A ring of reef enclosing a central lagoon. Land area approximately 4.5 square miles. Terrain low and flat. The interior dense with buka scrub and ren trees (Tournefortia argentea) — low, salt-tolerant, spreading canopy. The reef flat extending several hundred meters at low tide, surface of exposed coral and shallow pools. The southeastern shore faces the open Pacific. July 1937: uninhabited.
assets.notes: Lies approximately 400 miles southeast of Howland Island, along the 157-degree bearing of Noonan's sun line. The Nikumaroro hypothesis: if Earhart flew the sun line south-southeast after missing Howland, the aircraft's remaining fuel at 150 mph was sufficient to reach this island. The USS Colorado search aircraft noted signs of recent habitation here on July 9, 1937.

children.name: Nikumaroro_Southeast_Shore_1940
children.physique: The southeastern shore of Nikumaroro, where the land meets the reef flat. Ren trees providing shade at the interior edge — a single-tree shade that moves through the day with the sun, marking time like a sundial. At the boundary where the ren trees thin toward the reef flat: exposed coral, the sun unmediated, the terrain rough and difficult. The reef flat beyond, extending toward the open Pacific. This is the area Gallagher's resettlement colonists avoided — coral too rough, shade too thin.
children.notes: Where Gallagher found the partial human remains, woman's shoe, man's shoe, sextant box, and Benedictine bottle in September 1940. Three years after the disappearance.

children.name: Nikumaroro_Ren_Tree_Site_1940
children.physique: A single ren tree (Tournefortia argentea) standing in open ground on the southeastern shore — a low, spreading, salt-tolerant tree with gnarled branches and a canopy of oval leaves. The shade beneath it is a moving circle that shifts as the sun moves. The trunk of a second tree approximately 40 meters closer to the shore: numbers scratched into the bark with a fingernail or piece of shell, not carved — scratched. The numbers: 157, 337. Not letters. Numbers.
children.notes: The ren tree where Gallagher sat after finding the bones and watched the shade move. The second tree where he found the scratched numbers he copied into his notebook without knowing they were a sun line. His letter describes sitting beneath the tree long enough to watch the shade move.

children.name: Nikumaroro_Seven_Site_1980s
children.physique: The northeastern part of Nikumaroro, in an area the resettlement colonists called the Seven Site. A remnant campfire site visible as a dark soil discoloration. Nearby: a glass jar of a size consistent with 1930s commercial cosmetics packaging, partially buried in soil and leaf litter, the glass weathered but intact. Laboratory analysis of residue inside: mercuric chloride consistent with 1930s freckle cream preparations.
children.notes: Found by a researcher in the 1980s. Mercuric chloride was a commercial freckle treatment sold in the United States in the 1930s. Amelia Earhart was documented to have had freckles and used a freckle preparation. The island had not been permanently inhabited since the early 20th century.

children.name: Nikumaroro_Lagoon_2020
children.physique: The enclosed lagoon at the center of Nikumaroro atoll. Shallow water — clear above the sediment layer, the bottom visible from above. The Taraia Peninsula juts into the lagoon from the southern end. Near the Taraia Peninsula: a sediment-covered anomaly visible in satellite imagery analysis. The object's dimensions consistent with the fuselage of a Lockheed Model 10-E Electra. The surface reflective in the spectral analysis — consistent with aluminum. Covered by sediment. Waiting.
children.notes: Identified in satellite imagery analysis in 2020. Approximately the right size for the Electra fuselage. A research expedition was planned for November 2025 but permit difficulties and cyclone season pushed departure to July 2026. The object has not been examined. It is there.

children.name: Nikumaroro_Reef_Flat_1937
children.physique: The western reef flat of Nikumaroro at low tide — exposed coral extending several hundred meters from the shoreline, the surface a rough broken plane of bleached coral heads and shallow tidal pools. The flat is hard — not sand, not soil, but the compressed calcium structure of dead reef. At low tide the flat is walkable, if brutal on footwear. The Pacific swell breaks on the outer reef edge, white water on the horizon line. The interior lagoon to one side, shallow and calm. The western shore's gentler terrain versus the southeastern shore's rough coral where the remains were found.
children.notes: The terrain the evidence points to for any emergency landing — the reef flat is the only surface long enough and flat enough to have held the Electra. The script notes the woman's shoe 'had walked on coral.' This is that coral. A DP location for establishing the physical reality of the island as a possible landing site.

children.name: Nikumaroro_Interior_Ren_Forest_1937
children.physique: The interior of Nikumaroro — the dense growth of ren trees (Tournefortia argentea) and buka scrub that covers the island's interior. The canopy low and spreading, the branches gnarled and salt-pruned into horizontal shapes. Light filtering through the canopy: dappled, amber-warm, the equatorial sun broken into patches. The ground beneath: leaf litter, coral rubble, the accumulated debris of a forest floor that has been here without human interference for decades. The sound: wind through the canopy, the distant break of surf on the outer reef, no human sounds.
children.notes: The interior that sheltered anyone who survived on the island — shade, protection from wind, concealment. The ren trees are the landmark Gallagher uses to navigate the island in his letter. This sub-location establishes the island as a survivable environment, not just a reef flat.

assets.name: Lae_Airfield_1937
assets.physique: A grass airstrip on the coast of Lae, New Guinea. A slight downhill grade toward the harbor edge at the runway's end — the harbor, and then the Pacific beyond it. The runway surface: grass on packed earth, the width of a single aircraft, with the tropical vegetation of New Guinea on either side. At the harbor end: nothing — the grade drops away to water, and beyond the harbor, the open Pacific begins. July morning air: warm, humid, the specific tropical heaviness of coastal New Guinea.
assets.notes: The last stop before Howland Island. 2,243 nautical miles of open ocean between here and the target. The Electra took off July 2, 1937, loaded to maximum — 1,100 gallons of fuel. At the runway's end it descended to within 6 feet of the harbor surface before the airspeed built enough for the wing to assert itself against the weight.

children.name: Lae_Runway_Departure_End_1937
children.physique: The harbor end of the Lae grass runway — the point at which the packed-earth strip ends and the harbor begins. The runway dropping away in a slight grade to the harbor's edge, then nothing: harbor water, and beyond it the open Pacific. A crowd of onlookers visible at the runway margins — small figures at the edge of tropical vegetation, watching. The Lockheed Electra, silver in the morning light, heavy with fuel, at or past this point in its takeoff roll, descending slightly as the gear leaves the ground, the wing not yet generating enough lift to climb. The harbor water below the landing gear: six feet of clearance.
children.notes: The script is specific: 'The wheels left the ground and the aircraft sank toward the water, heavy with fuel and the physics of a wing not yet generating sufficient lift at the speed it had achieved at the runway's end.' This is the moment of maximum weight and minimum margin — the physical beginning of the 20-hour flight.

children.name: Lae_Hangar_Preflight_1937
children.physique: The hangar area at Lae airfield in the hours before departure — a corrugated metal or open-sided tropical hangar structure, the Electra being serviced, fuel being loaded through access panels in the fuselage. Ground crew in working clothes appropriate to tropical New Guinea. The fuel tanker or drums. Fuel hose connections to the aircraft's fill points. The aircraft sitting low on its gear from the weight — 1,100 gallons of aviation fuel is visible weight, the aircraft's silhouette lower than normal, the suspension compressed. The tropical morning: humid, warm, the light flat before the sun rises fully.
children.notes: The preparation scene — establishing the weight, the fuel, the physical reality of what the aircraft is being asked to do. The 1,100-gallon fuel load that is the flight's only resource and its only clock.

assets.name: NRL_Washington_1953
assets.physique: A research office at the Naval Research Laboratory in Washington, DC. A government scientist's workspace in the early 1950s — a metal desk with papers organized into working stacks, a typewriter, mechanical pencils and pencil sharpeners, graph paper with propagation curves plotted by hand. Filing cabinets. A wall of bookshelves holding technical reports bound in government grey. Fluorescent overhead lighting. The specific atmosphere of a classified government research facility: institutional, unhurried, the quiet of work that proceeds on its own internal schedule.
assets.notes: Where the unnamed NRL researcher produced his retrospective analysis of Pacific radio propagation anomalies. His appendix on the Earhart case — the one that asked 'Then what was it?' in a marginal pencil note — was excluded from partial declassification and never published.

children.name: NRL_Desk_Appendix_Close_1953
children.physique: A close view of the NRL researcher's metal desk surface — specifically the appendix pages of the study, separated from the main report body by a paperclip. The main report visible under the separated appendix: a bound government technical document on Naval Research Laboratory letterhead. The appendix pages: typed single-spaced, technical terminology, propagation curves in the margin. At the bottom of a page: a pencil marginal note in a private hand, not part of the typed text. Four words: 'Then what was it?' The pencil mark slightly softer than the typewriter type — a human hand alongside the institutional machine. A mechanical pencil resting on the desk beside the document.
children.notes: The marginal note is the script's climactic object in the NRL section. The paperclip separating the appendix from the main report is a physical fact with narrative weight — this is the document that was excluded from declassification. A close shot of the desk with the note visible is the DP shot.

children.name: NRL_Filing_Cabinet_1953
children.physique: A row of government-issue steel filing cabinets in the NRL research office — grey-green institutional paint, brass drawer handles, each drawer labeled with classification markings and date ranges in government typeface. One drawer partially open, a hanging folder visible with a classification stamp. The filing system of a mid-century classified government research facility: organized, institutional, the bureaucratic apparatus through which certain findings pass into official record and others do not. Fluorescent light overhead. The cabinets represent where the appendix went: filed, not published, not declassified.
children.notes: The institutional mechanism of burial — not dramatic suppression, just the ordinary filing apparatus that decides what enters the public record and what does not. The appendix was 'excluded from the partial declassification that eventually released the main report.' It is in a drawer like this one.

assets.name: Betty_Klenck_Home_1937
assets.physique: A private home in Saint Petersburg, Florida, in the summer of 1937. A room where the family shortwave radio is kept — a large wooden cabinet radio of the mid-1930s, the dial face illuminated by a warm amber glow, the speaker cloth visible behind a wooden grille. The room has the quality of a summer evening interior in a Florida home: the humidity present in the way fabrics hang, the particular warm light of incandescent bulbs. The shortwave radio's dial set to 3105 kHz. A spiral-bound or composition notebook open on the table beside the radio, a pencil moving across it.
assets.notes: Where Betty Klenck was listening on 3105 kHz in the days after the disappearance. She was 15 years old. She heard a woman's voice and wrote down what she believed she heard. The notebook was not publicized for decades. This location exists in the script as the civilian parallel to the official monitoring stations — a teenager with a family shortwave radio, writing.

children.name: Klenck_Radio_Dial_Close_1937
children.physique: The illuminated dial of a mid-1930s shortwave radio receiver — a curved glass face with frequency markings in the shortwave bands, the tuning needle positioned at 3105 kHz. The dial glows amber-warm from the internal indicator bulb. The cabinet wood surrounding it: dark walnut or mahogany veneer, the speaker grille cloth below. A hand — young, a teenager's hand — resting near the tuning knob. The static of the shortwave band audible in the scene's atmosphere if not in the image. The quality of 1930s home electronics: large, hand-built, the craftsmanship of an era before mass miniaturization.
children.notes: The civilian listening point. A 15-year-old's hand at a shortwave dial, set to the same frequency Leo Bellarts had been monitoring for eight hours. The frequency is the connecting thread between all the listeners in this episode.

children.name: Klenck_Notebook_Writing_Close_1937
children.physique: A notebook open beside the radio — a composition notebook or spiral pad, the pages slightly warped from Florida humidity. A teenager's handwriting moving across the page, not the economical shorthand of a trained radioman but the careful full-word transcription of someone writing down what they hear as they hear it. The page dated. The entries: a woman's voice, fragments, details that the writer transcribes without yet understanding their significance. The pencil moving. The radio audible in the background.
children.notes: The Betty Klenck notebook is a named object in the script and in the manifest. This sub-location is the DP moment of its creation — a young person writing down something she does not yet understand the importance of. The notebook is now held by a research organization. This is the moment before that.

assets.name: National_Archives_Washington_DC
assets.physique: The National Archives building in Washington, DC — a neoclassical stone structure, the interior reading rooms with long wooden tables and researcher lighting, archival boxes on trolleys, white cotton gloves worn by researchers. The archive's atmosphere: institutional preservation, the particular controlled humidity of a facility that holds paper for centuries. A document box labeled with archival information: 'Leo G. Bellarts Papers, 1937-1971.' Inside the box: folders, the radio log at the front of the collection — the original paper log sheet, preserved in archival enclosure, the pencil marks still present on slightly damp-textured paper.
assets.notes: Where the Itasca radio log now lives, donated by Bellarts. The script states: 'It is held there now, as part of the Leo G. Bellarts Papers, nineteen thirty-seven through nineteen seventy-one. Anyone who wants to read the last thing Amelia Earhart said to another human being can read it there.' The archive is where the record of the last transmission is publicly available — the democratic ending to the chain of custody.

children.name: National_Archives_Reading_Room
children.physique: The research reading room of the National Archives — long wooden tables under institutional overhead lighting, researchers seated with archival boxes before them, white cotton gloves required. The controlled-humidity air. An archival box open on a table: 'Leo G. Bellarts Papers, 1937-1971.' A researcher's hands, gloved, lifting the original radio log sheet from its archival folder — the paper of a log kept on a Coast Guard cutter in July 1937, the pencil marks still readable, the timestamps still sequential, the final entry at 0843 still followed by the blank space that means silence.
children.notes: The endpoint of the chain of custody: from Bellarts's radio room desk, through four decades of personal preservation, to the National Archives, to anyone who wants to read it. The script emphasizes this accessibility: 'Anyone who wants to read the last thing Amelia Earhart said to another human being can read it there.' The reading room is where that sentence becomes literal.

assets.name: Hoodless_Fiji_Office_1940
assets.physique: A colonial medical examination office in Fiji, 1940 — a professional medical workspace appropriate to a colonial British physician in a tropical posting. A metal examination table. A desk with official colonial health service stationery, a typewriter, ink bottles, a blotter. Natural light from a window appropriate to Fiji's tropics — bright, flat, slightly humid. On a side table: the skeletal remains sent from Nikumaroro, laid out for examination, partially complete. Hoodless's examination notes beside them — measurements being taken with a bone caliper, the numbers written in an official medical hand. The bones on the table. The instrument measuring them.
assets.notes: Where the only physical examination of the Nikumaroro remains occurred. Hoodless's conclusion was male. His measurements are the only physical evidence the case retains — the bones were subsequently lost. This location exists in the script as the place where the evidence that cannot be recovered was first assessed. The bones were here. Then they weren't.

children.name: Hoodless_Examination_Table_Close_1940
children.physique: The examination table in Hoodless's Fiji office — partial skeletal remains laid out in approximate anatomical order, some elements missing. A bone caliper open beside a long bone, the measurement being taken. Hoodless's written form beside the remains: a grid of measurements in ink, the physician's methodical recording of dimensions. The remains themselves: bleached, weathered from years of exposure on a tropical island, smaller than a complete adult skeleton because they are partial. The caliper measuring what still exists. The numbers being written. After this moment, the bones were set aside, moved, and eventually lost.
children.notes: The sole physical examination of the Nikumaroro remains. Two 21st-century forensic analyses were conducted on the numbers Hoodless wrote here, reaching opposite conclusions. The bones are gone. The numbers remain. This is where the numbers were made.

assets.name: USS_Colorado_Search_1937
assets.physique: The USS Colorado (BB-45) — a battleship operating in the central Pacific, July 9, 1937, as part of the largest air-sea search in American history to that date. The Colorado's deck: a broad steel surface with the superstructure rising amidships, catapults for float planes mounted on either side of the main turrets. Three Vought O3U Corsair floatplanes aboard, one of which flew over Nikumaroro that morning. The Pacific horizon around the vessel: open ocean in every direction, the Phoenix Islands group in the search sector. Morning light. The search pattern being flown: grid squares, each square representing a portion of ocean to be assessed from the air.
assets.notes: One of nine ships assigned to the search. On July 9, 1937, a float plane from the Colorado flew over Nikumaroro and filed a report noting 'signs of recent habitation' on an uninhabited island. The search moved elsewhere. The file note was made. The conclusion was: nothing found anywhere.

children.name: Colorado_Floatplane_Over_Nikumaroro_1937
children.physique: A Vought O3U Corsair floatplane at low altitude over Nikumaroro Island — the island visible below, its ring of reef, the central lagoon, the ren tree interior, the southeastern shore. The floatplane's perspective: looking down at an island that appears uninhabited — no smoke, no visible aircraft, no signal fire. The reef flat visible from altitude. The lagoon's surface. The island's terrain from above: low, flat, coral and scrub. In one area: something that reads as 'signs of recent habitation' in the pilot's language — a darkened area, disturbed ground, something that departs from the island's baseline. The floatplane continuing on its search pattern.
children.notes: The pilot filed a report using the phrase 'signs of recent habitation.' On an uninhabited island. The search moved to the next grid square. Seven days after the disappearance, someone on this island may have been alive to observe the floatplane pass overhead.

assets.name: Lockheed_Electra_NR16020_1937
assets.physique: A Lockheed Model 10-E Electra twin-engine aluminum aircraft, registration NR16020. Approximately 55 feet wingspan, 38 feet length. Polished aluminum skin with rounded fuselage — the streamlined form of 1930s American aviation design. Two Pratt and Whitney Wasp radial engines, each mounted in a nacelle on the leading edge of the low wing, each rated at 600 horsepower, each driving a variable-pitch propeller. Extended-range fuel tanks filling the fuselage interior behind the firewall and in the wing — 1,100 gallons total at Lae departure. A wooden partition dividing the fuselage: cockpit forward, navigation space aft. The aircraft's silver surface catching equatorial morning light.
assets.notes: The aircraft Earhart flew on the world circumnavigation attempt. Call sign KHAQQ. Loaded to near maximum certification weight at Lae departure — 1,100 gallons of fuel. At departure it descended to within 6 feet of the harbor water. At cruise: approximately 145 mph, burning 12-14 gallons per engine per hour. Last known position: somewhere on the 157/337 sun line, near Howland Island, at 0843 on July 2, 1937.

assets.name: Itasca_Radio_Log_1937
assets.physique: A paper log sheet on a radio room desk, slightly damp from Pacific humidity — the pencil marks slightly softer than they would be on dry paper, more decisive. Timestamped entries in the abbreviated functional shorthand of a working radioman, written as transmissions arrive. The critical entries: 0742 — signal strength S-five, the needle pinned at maximum, the transmission partial: 'KHAQQ calling Itasca. We must be on you but cannot see you but gas is running low. Been unable to reach you by radio. We are flying at one thousand feet.' Then 0758. Then 0800. Then 0843 — the last entry. After 0843: silence.
assets.notes: Kept by Leo Bellarts not because the Navy required it but because he recognized immediately what it contained. He preserved it for decades. Donated to the National Archives as part of the Leo G. Bellarts Papers, 1937-1971. Anyone who wants to read the last thing Amelia Earhart said to another human being can read it there.

assets.name: Noonan_Sun_Line_Chart_1937
assets.physique: A navigation chart of the central Pacific — paper, spread on the navigation table in the aft fuselage of the Electra, weighted at corners against vibration. On the chart: a line drawn through or near the position of Howland Island at two bearings — 157 degrees running southeast toward the Phoenix Islands, and 337 degrees running northwest toward the Marshall Islands. The line represents the sun line: the aircraft is somewhere on this thread. The handwriting marking the line is steady — trained by years of work to remain steady because unsteady hands produce numbers that end flights. Two numbers in that hand: 157. 337.
assets.notes: Noonan's last reliable celestial calculation. Passed forward through the gap in the partition as a handwritten note. Earhart reported the numbers on the radio at 0843 — they became the last position data in the Itasca's log. Extended 400 miles southeast, the 157-degree bearing passes through or near Nikumaroro.

assets.name: Bubble_Sextant_1937
assets.physique: A bubble sextant — a precision navigation instrument designed for aerial use. Brass and steel construction in a fitted leather case. A small artificial bubble replaces the natural sea horizon, allowing celestial shots when the real horizon is obscured by cloud, darkness, or haze. An eyepiece for sighting the sun or stars. Graduated arc for measuring the angle of the celestial body above the artificial horizon. The instrument that substitutes for the absent real world when the Pacific has no edges and no markers and the horizon does not exist in any practical sense.
assets.notes: Noonan's primary navigation instrument. Used to produce the sun line. The sky has not been entirely clear. The sun line is all he has.

assets.name: Sextant_Box_Gardner_Island_1940
assets.physique: A wooden instrument case of the type used to store a marine sextant — wooden construction with brass fittings and a hinged lid, interior lined with fitted velvet or felt molded to hold the instrument. The case shows weathering from exposure and time — the wood bleached and cracked by sun and salt air, the brass fittings oxidized to dull green, the lining compressed and stained. No instrument inside it. The case alone, on the southeastern shore of Nikumaroro.
assets.notes: Found by Gallagher in September 1940 near the partial human remains on the southeastern shore. A sextant box on an uninhabited island, with a woman's shoe, a man's shoe, and a Benedictine bottle. Gallagher sent the bones and artifacts to Fiji for examination. The bones were subsequently lost. The sextant box's provenance was never formally established.

assets.name: Benedictine_Bottle_1940
assets.physique: A glass bottle of the shape and size associated with Benedictine liqueur — a distinctive bottle with a slightly irregular shape compared to common bottles of the era, green glass with an embossed label area, weathered by years of exposure on a tropical island. Empty. The glass salt-etched on the exterior, the interior surface still faintly colored from its original contents.
assets.notes: Found with the remains and sextant box on the southeastern shore of Nikumaroro. Noted in Gallagher's official report. The bottle's presence on an island with no permanent habitation since the early 20th century is unexplained by any alternative hypothesis.

assets.name: Worn_Womans_Shoe_1940
assets.physique: A single leather shoe of a style consistent with 1930s American women's practical footwear — low-heeled, lace-up, leather upper and leather sole. The shoe has been worn for a very long time by someone who had no other shoe. The leather has shaped itself to the foot — the sole worn unevenly in the pattern of someone's particular gait, the upper creased in the specific geography of someone's foot. It has walked on coral. The leather is bleached and cracked from sun and salt exposure, but the shape of the foot that wore it is still present in the leather.
assets.notes: Gallagher's letter to his sister describes it precisely: 'It was a shoe that had been worn for a very long time by someone who had no other shoe. The leather had shaped itself to the foot. It had walked on coral.' Found with the partial remains, man's shoe, sextant box, and Benedictine bottle.

assets.name: Freckle_Cream_Jar_1980s
assets.physique: A small glass cosmetics jar of the type common to 1930s American commercial packaging — cylindrical, approximately 2-3 inches diameter, clear or pale green glass, a threaded neck for a screw-top lid, the lid absent or separate. The glass weathered from decades of exposure on the island — exterior surface salt-etched, interior showing residue of the original preparation. Laboratory analysis: the residue is mercuric chloride, consistent with commercial freckle cream formulations of the 1930s United States market.
assets.notes: Found by a researcher in the 1980s near a remnant campfire site in the northeastern part of Nikumaroro (Seven Site area). Amelia Earhart was documented to have had freckles and to have used a freckle preparation. The island had no permanent habitation since the early 20th century.

assets.name: OHare_Diary_1937
assets.physique: A small personal diary kept in a seabag during a Coast Guard posting. Standard sailor's personal notebook — small enough to fit in a jacket pocket, covers worn from the seabag, pages slightly damp from Pacific shipboard humidity. The handwriting of a 23-year-old man writing quickly, off-shift, not for publication. July 2 entry: 'The static sounds different when you're waiting for someone. It has a shape. The shape of the voice that should be in it.' July 4 entry: 'It was not skip. I have been listening to skip for four years. Skip does not say words.'
assets.notes: Not an official document. A private record of a young radioman who knew the difference between a dead channel and a live one, and between atmospheric skip and signal-shaped absence. His off-shift monitoring of 3105 kHz produced a possible transmission at 0300 on July 4. The duty officer logged it as skip. O'Hare did not.

assets.name: NRL_Propagation_Study_1953
assets.physique: A bound government technical report on Naval Research Laboratory letterhead — the main document running to dozens of pages with graphs of propagation curves, atmospheric data tables, and statistical analysis. Appended to the main report: a secondary analysis of the Earhart case, typed single-spaced with technical terminology. In the margin of the appendix, in pencil, in a private hand not part of the official text: four words — 'Then what was it?' The appendix pages separated from the main report by a paperclip. The main report released in partial declassification. The appendix excluded.
assets.notes: The appendix finding: atmospheric conditions on July 2-5, 1937 in the central Pacific were normal. The Itasca's transmissions should have been receivable by any properly functioning receiver within 500 miles. The asymmetry documented in the Itasca log was not atmospheric in origin. If the radio worked and the atmosphere was clear — and both are established — then the failure was somewhere in the channel itself. The study was never published.

assets.name: Noonan_Handwritten_Note_157_337
assets.physique: A small slip of paper — folded once or twice to fit through the gap in the Electra's partition. The paper is aircraft-paper, thin and practical, from the navigation table's supply. On one face, in a steady hand: two numbers. Not an equation. Not a narrative. Two numbers, one above the other or side by side: 157. 337. The handwriting is the specific quality the script describes — steady, trained, the product of a hand that has been disciplined to remain steady because unsteady hands produce numbers that end flights. Eighteen hours of turbulence and engine vibration have done nothing to the hand that produced these numbers. The paper is slightly cold from altitude. The fold crease in it from being passed through the gap.
assets.notes: The handwritten note Noonan passed forward through the partition gap to Earhart. The script makes this a named narrative object: 'His handwriting — and this matters, this is a specific thing, not a decoration — is steady.' The numbers on this note became the last position data Earhart broadcast. They are in the Itasca's log. They point 400 miles southeast to Nikumaroro.

assets.name: OHare_Reception_Report_1937
assets.physique: An official Coast Guard or Navy radio monitoring report form, filled out in O'Hare's hand — the standard operational report for a possible radio reception event. The form's fields: date (July 4, 1937), time (0300), frequency (3105 kHz), signal character (voice, possible), content (partial, unresolved into words). The notation at the bottom of the form in a different hand — the duty officer's notation: 'Atmospheric skip.' The form filed. The duty officer's handwriting more authoritative on the form than O'Hare's, the institutional determination overwriting the personal observation. The form as a physical object: carbon paper copies, the official routing stamps.
assets.notes: The report O'Hare filed on the possible transmission at 0300 on July 4. The duty officer logged it as atmospheric skip. O'Hare's diary entry that night: 'It was not skip. I have been listening to skip for four years. Skip does not say words.' The report is the official record. The diary is the unofficial one. Both survive.

assets.name: PanAm_Routing_Memo_1937
assets.physique: An internal Pan American Airways memorandum on company letterhead — the crisp formal stationery of a major corporation in the 1930s, the Pan American Airways System logo at the top. Dated July 5, 1937. From the Chief Communications Officer, San Francisco. To: All Pacific Station Managers. Subject: Monitoring, 3105 kHz. The text of the memo professional and adequate — a corporate order with a stated rationale. The operative sentence: 'Discontinue monitoring. File as unconfirmed atmospheric phenomena.' The memo routed through the Pacific station network: Midway, Wake Island, Honolulu. Distribution stamps on the routing copy. The last instruction to stop listening.
assets.notes: The script describes this memo at length: 'Pan American Airways' chief communications officer in San Francisco sent a routing memo to the Pacific station managers on July fifth, nineteen thirty-seven. The memo instructed all Pacific stations to discontinue monitoring three thousand one hundred and five kilohertz effective immediately.' The script notes: 'The stated reason is adequate and logical.' It then says: 'They were told to stop listening.' The memo is the physical object that issued that instruction.

assets.name: Betty_Klenck_Notebook_1937
assets.physique: A teenager's notebook — a composition book or spiral-bound pad, the pages slightly warped from Florida humidity. The handwriting inside a 15-year-old girl's hand: careful, full-word transcription, the writing of someone recording something that feels important but whose importance is not yet fully legible. Dated entries in the days after July 2, 1937. The content: fragments of a woman's voice heard on a shortwave radio set to 3105 kHz. Details written down without context, details that researchers note are consistent with circumstances of the flight the writer would have had no knowledge of in 1937. The notebook not publicized for decades. Now held by a research organization.
assets.notes: Named in the script alongside the official monitoring reports: 'A fifteen-year-old girl in Saint Petersburg, Florida, named Betty Klenck, was listening to her family's shortwave radio. She had the dial on three one oh five. She heard a woman's voice, and she wrote in her notebook what she believed she heard.' The notebook is the civilian parallel to Bellarts's radio log — both are records of someone writing down what they heard on 3105 kHz. One is in the National Archives. One is held by a research organization.

assets.name: Bellarts_Goerner_Letter_1961
assets.physique: A personal letter from Leo Bellarts to Fred Goerner, a journalist and researcher investigating the Earhart disappearance — written in 1961, twenty-four years after the event. The letter on personal stationery or plain paper, the handwriting of a man in his late 40s, deliberate and considered. The relevant passage: Earhart was 'peacefully on the bottom of the sea, no farther than one hundred miles from Howland.' The word 'peacefully' carrying the weight of a man who has spent twenty-four years reconciling two facts — a maximum-strength signal and an empty sky — and arrived at the most merciful conclusion the evidence would support. The letter written to a researcher, not for the public record.
assets.notes: The script quotes this letter directly: 'In a letter written in nineteen sixty-one to Fred Goerner, a journalist and researcher who was investigating the disappearance, Bellarts wrote that Earhart was — peacefully on the bottom of the sea, no farther than one hundred miles from Howland.' The script then says: 'He believed this. He also kept the log.' Both things are true simultaneously — Bellarts's belief and his preservation of the evidence that complicates the belief.

assets.name: Hoodless_Bone_Measurements_1940
assets.physique: D.W. Hoodless's written examination record of the Nikumaroro skeletal remains — official medical documentation on British colonial health service forms or institutional paper, the measurements written in ink in a physician's careful hand. A grid of numbers: bone lengths in centimeters, diameters at measured intervals, ratios and proportions recorded as the examination standard of 1940 medicine required. The document is not dramatic — it is methodical, institutional, the record of a medical examination conducted with the tools and methods of its era. It describes a skeleton that no longer exists. The numbers are all that remain of the physical evidence.
assets.notes: The script: 'The bones were set aside. They were not returned to Nikumaroro, not archived with particular care, not treated as historically significant. They were examined, catalogued, and then — in the way that material without an official claim tends to move — they were lost. The measurements survived.' Two 21st-century forensic analyses were conducted on these numbers, reaching opposite conclusions. The bones are gone. These numbers are the only physical evidence the case retains.

assets.name: Colorado_Floatplane_Search_Report_1937
assets.physique: A standard military aviation search report filed by the pilot of a USS Colorado floatplane after overflying Nikumaroro Island on July 9, 1937. Official Navy report form, the pilot's observations entered in standard search-pilot terminology: negative contact, island appeared uninhabited, no wreckage visible, no distress signals. And then, in the notation section, in the language used for objects that depart from baseline: 'signs of recent habitation.' On an island identified as uninhabited. The report filed with the search coordination effort. The search moved to the next grid square.
assets.notes: The script: 'One of the float planes flew over Nikumaroro. The pilot filed a report. Standard language. The island appeared uninhabited. No wreckage visible. No signs of distress. The report noted, in the standard terminology of a search pilot cataloguing a negative contact: signs of recent habitation.' The phrase 'signs of recent habitation' in an official Navy search report, on a documented uninhabited island, seven days after the disappearance.

assets.name: Gallagher_Sister_Letter_1940
assets.physique: A personal letter written by Gerald Gallagher to his sister in Ireland in October 1940, never sent. The letter on personal stationery, the handwriting of a 27-year-old British colonial administrator writing informally to family — not the careful official language of his commission report, but the full account of what he found and felt. The passages the script quotes: a description of the ren tree and its moving shade, the description of the woman's shoe, the description of the numbers scratched into the second tree — 157, 337 — which he copied into his notebook without knowing what they were. The letter found among his effects after his death at 29. Shipped to his family by the colonial administration. His sister's address in Ireland.
assets.notes: The letter the script reads from directly: 'There is another thing I did not report. Approximately forty meters from the bones, closer to the shore, I found marks on the trunk of a second tree. Not carved — scratched. With a fingernail or a piece of shell. I could not read them. They were not letters. They were numbers. I copied them into my notebook. They read: one five seven, three three seven.' Gallagher had no context for a sun line. He copied the numbers because they were there. He died on the island before anyone could ask him what else he had seen.
